title: Password manager fundamentals
body_md:
## Make every site a separate secret

A password manager stores and generates credentials so that you can use a different password at every site. Its value is containment: if a small shop leaks one password, it should not open your email. A manager can be a reputable browser or platform feature or a separate app; compare its security and recovery design rather than assuming one category is always safe.

### How the vault changes login

Create a long, unique primary passphrase you can actually retain. Secure a synced vault with the strongest MFA it supports and protect every device that can unlock it. Let the generator create a distinct password for each account, and save the **verified** site address with the record. Before changing a password, confirm which account you are in and that the new entry really saved; test sign-in on a trusted device before deleting an old record. For a work account, follow the employer's approved storage policy.

Autofill can be a useful warning when a saved login does not match the current site. It is not a verdict: forms, subdomains, app links and manager settings can also stop a fill on a legitimate page, while permissive matching settings can fill too broadly. If fill fails, pause, inspect the full address and open the service independently. Do not manually paste a high-value password into an unfamiliar form to “fix” it.

### Plan for failure as well as convenience

The vault concentrates access. Malware or an unlocked shared device can defeat much of its protection; a weak or reused primary passphrase is dangerous. Learn the product's recovery method **before** relying on it: some services cannot recover vault contents when the decryption secret is lost, while others provide account recovery with different trade-offs. Keep an offline recovery plan appropriate to that product and a trusted person if needed. Never leave a plaintext CSV export in Downloads or cloud sharing: if you migrate, protect the file, confirm the import, then remove the temporary plaintext copy securely under your device policy.

Start with primary email and financial accounts. Replace reused passwords in a manageable sequence, then expand to other sites. You do not need to change every untouched unique password on a calendar. Change a secret when it is compromised, reused, weak, or required by the service. A manager reduces password reuse; it cannot make a fake page safe or repair an infected device.

widget_config.goal: Set up a manager so each important account has a unique password and a tested recovery path.
widget_config.today_action: Choose one trusted manager, secure its primary account, and migrate one high-value login using a generated unique password; verify the saved entry before ending the session.
widget_config.scope: General education; product features and employer policies differ. UK NCSC organisational criteria are adapted as consumer questions. Checked 2026-10-20.

blocks.title: Autofill missing on a copied checkout
blocks.situation: A synthetic store message opens `checkout.support-example.test`. The saved store login does not appear, and the page asks for the vault password instead.
blocks.analysis: The new address and request for the vault’s primary secret are strong reasons to stop. Open the store from your own bookmark, inspect the account there, and never type the vault passphrase into a store checkout.

blocks.title: Real service redesigned its sign-in form
blocks.situation: A synthetic university moves sign-in to a documented single-sign-on subdomain. Your manager does not fill, but the university’s own help page links that subdomain.
blocks.analysis: A missing fill alone does not prove fraud. Verify the change through the university’s independently opened site or IT channel; update the saved login matching only after you have confirmed the destination.

blocks.title: Move one account into a vault
blocks.setup: Synthetic example: you are migrating a community-market account to a manager on a personal laptop.

steps.prompt: The manager offers a random password for the account. What should you save?

choices.text: The generated password together with the confirmed site address.
choices.consequence: The account gets an independent secret tied to its real destination.
choices.explanation: Uniqueness prevents reuse; an accurately saved address helps future matching.

choices.text: Your familiar password with one new symbol.
choices.consequence: The pattern may remain reused or predictable.
choices.explanation: A small edit does not reliably separate this account from old secrets.

steps.prompt: After changing it, the manager seems not to have saved the new entry. What next?

choices.text: Check the vault record and test a fresh sign-in while the account session still works.
choices.consequence: You confirm the new secret before relying on it.
choices.explanation: A successful change page does not prove the manager stored the exact value.

choices.text: Log out everywhere and trust that sync will eventually restore it.
choices.explanation: Verify the saved credential and sync before ending the working session.

steps.prompt: A later login form does not autofill. What interpretation is safest?

choices.text: Pause, inspect the address and reach the service independently before editing match settings.
choices.consequence: A harmless form change and a fake site remain distinguishable.
choices.explanation: Autofill is a clue, not an absolute security decision.

choices.text: Paste the password manually because managers often fail.
choices.consequence: The unfamiliar form could receive the password.
choices.explanation: Manual entry defeats the opportunity to check the destination.

steps.prompt: You export a CSV to switch managers. What closes the migration?

choices.text: Verify the new import, then remove the unencrypted export from temporary storage under your device policy.
choices.consequence: The temporary plaintext copy no longer sits exposed.
choices.explanation: An export may contain the entire vault in readable form.

choices.text: Keep the CSV in a shared cloud folder as a convenient backup.
choices.consequence: Anyone with folder access may read all credentials.
choices.explanation: Use the manager’s supported secure backup or recovery method instead.

blocks.debrief: A manager solves the reuse problem when the saved site, generated secret, vault protection and recovery plan are all checked. Retry the step where you accepted uncertainty.

questions.prompt: A trusted site changes its sign-in subdomain and autofill stops. What should you do?

choices.text: Verify the subdomain through the service’s own independent channel before updating the saved match.
choices.explanation: Legitimate form changes exist; confirm the destination first.

choices.text: Assume no fill always proves phishing.
choices.explanation: Managers can fail to match real forms and subdomains.

questions.prompt: Why is a plaintext vault export sensitive?

choices.text: It can expose many accounts at once outside the vault’s normal protections.
choices.explanation: Migration copies need a short, controlled lifetime.

choices.text: It only contains usernames, never passwords.
choices.explanation: CSV exports may include readable passwords.

choices.text: A long, unique phrase protected by the manager’s supported MFA and recovery plan.
choices.explanation: The vault deserves an independent secret and tested access plan.

choices.text: The password already used for email so it is easy to remember.
choices.explanation: Reuse couples the two most important accounts.
